newsitem.title: USA: Top U.S. antitrust officials to soothe EU bruises.
newsitem.headline: Top U.S. antitrust officials to soothe EU bruises.

text.p: President Bill Clinton praised the European Union's resolution on Wednesday of the Boeing -McDonnell Douglas deal, as top antitrust officials moved quickly to patch up bruised relations with their European counterparts.
"I am pleased that Boeing and the EU have resolved their differences," Clinton said in a written statement. "We hope that the EU will give the merger final approval expeditiously."

For the president, the EU decision marked a foreign policy victory: "The Boeing-McDonnell Douglas merger will promote consolidation and efficiency in the U.S. defence industry and preserve the jobs of 14,000 workers at Douglas Aircraft Co."
He said nothing about the European Consortium, Airbus Industrie, which many American politicians blamed for the EU's reluctance to approve the deal.

U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said Clinton reminded the Europeans that their analysis should focus solely on the competitive issues involved, and not on "trade policy, industrial policy and extraneous politics."

"The president made very clear that while of course we would not seek a trade war with the European Union ... we would not tolerate political interference with one of the great exporters of this country," she told CNN's "Moneyline" programme.

In fact, American politicians excoriated the EU and held out the U.S. Federal Trade Commission as the proper forum for consideration of the deal. The FTC cleared the $15 billion merger earlier this month.

The European Commission, the European Union's 20-member executive body, recommended the deal on Wednesday after the Seattle-based aircraft maker offered last-minute concessions. Antitrust experts from the bloc's 15 countries are now expected to review the merger by next week.

Two top antitrust officials in the United States on Wednesday looked to reinforce traditional cooperation that has marked the enforcement of competition policy, after a crisis that put their relationship with the EU at risk.
The assistant attorney general in charge of antitrust, Joel Klein, who met in Brussels with the Europeans on behalf of the administration, said the two sides needed to learn to work together better.

"When you have an experience that is stressful and difficult (you need) to make sure you learn what you can and see if you can avoid those kinds of problems in the future," he said in a telephone interview.
Robert Pitofsky, chairman of the Federal Trade Commission took pains to point out similarities in outlook between the EU and FTC on the Boeing deal.

Pitofsky said that the EU "agreed with the essential point that led a majority of the FTC to clear the deal -- that Douglas no longer constituted a competitive force in selling large commerical planes to airlines."
Like the European Union, the Federal Trade Commission found troublng the exclusive provider contracts Boeing had with three airlines.

But while the Europeans made the agreements a sticking point under their law, American legal precedents have always required that if exclusive contracts amount to less than 30 percent of a market they are not a problem. In this case, the exclusive contracts amounted to 11-12 percent of business.
"They have a different law and different precedents," said Pitofsky.

At this point, the Americans and Europeans are on the verge of signing a new agreement -- the "positive comity" agreement -- so that each can refer problems to the other. Pitofsky and Klein said they expect that agreement to stay on track. The agreement does not cover mergers.
